title: Stop asking AI to make the old thing faster
notes: Emphasis markup: [[word]] renders in the accent yellow. Use on two slides per set at most.

slides.headline: Two kinds of AI.
slides.deck: [[Efficiency AI]] makes the same article faster. [[Opportunity AI]] gives readers something they never had before.

slides.headline: Your archive is a product now.
slides.deck: Nursing Times built an answer engine that draws only on its own archive. More than 200,000 questions since 2024. About 100 subscriptions traced directly to it.

slides.text: of the questions put to Nursing Times' answer engine came from suggested questions embedded in articles. Readers want the next answer right where they already are.

slides.deck: Every time The Texas Tribune's school voucher chatbot said it, the question went to the reporting team. The first one became a story.

slides.headline: A reporter, a phone and an AI pipeline that cuts the footage to 60 seconds. That's a video desk now.
slides.deck: NLW built one for The AI Daily Brief with Claude. He isn't a coder.

slides.headline: Many will fail. That's fine.
slides.deck: Four local outlets built chatbots for about $40 a month with a University of North Carolina research center. 185 queries in 45 days. Three of the four dropped theirs.

items: Do readers get something new, or the same thing faster?
Could you have afforded to try it a year ago?
Does it make your reporters more visible, or less?

slides.text: Stop asking how much faster AI can make the [[old thing]]. Start asking what your readers would do with the [[new one]].

slides.question: What could your readers get from you that they never could before?
